p3samples9: Why do some people prefer reading books to watching films?

I think it's mainly about the kind of involvement each one demands. A book leaves a lot of room for imagination: you decide what the characters look and sound like, so the story feels partly your own creation. Books also give you access to a character's inner thoughts in a way film rarely can, which makes them better suited to complex, introspective stories. And reading is self-paced; you can pause, reread a line, reflect. Films, by contrast, are more immediate and often more emotionally powerful in the moment. So it's not that one is superior. They simply reward different kinds of attention.
Do you think printed books will disappear?

I doubt it, at least not in the foreseeable future. People predicted their death when e-readers first appeared, but sales of printed books have held up surprisingly well. I think that's because print offers things screens don't: no notifications, no eye strain, and the simple pleasure of owning a physical object. That said, the market will probably keep shifting. Reference books and textbooks are increasingly digital, and audiobooks are growing rapidly. So printed books might become more of a choice than a default, especially for fiction and gifts, but I can't see them disappearing.

The programme I'd like to talk about is a cooking documentary series called "Chef's Table", which is available on a streaming platform. Each episode focuses on a single chef somewhere in the world, often someone who's quite famous in culinary circles but almost unknown to the general public.

What sets it apart from most food shows is that it isn't really about recipes. You hardly ever see step-by-step instructions. Instead, each episode tells the story of how that person came to cook the way they do: their childhood, the setbacks they faced, what they're trying to say through their food. Some of the episodes are surprisingly emotional, a chef who opened a restaurant after losing almost everything, for instance, or one who's trying to revive ingredients that her grandmother used to cook with.

I don't watch it in any regular way; it's not something I binge. I tend to save an episode for a quiet evening when I want something that's absorbing but not stressful, maybe once or twice a month. And I usually watch it with my partner, which has turned out to be a bit dangerous, because at least three episodes have ended with us booking a table somewhere we can't really afford.

So why do I enjoy it? Partly, it's simply beautiful to look at. The cinematography is gorgeous, with lots of slow-motion shots and classical music, which some people find a bit pretentious, and I can see why, but I love it. More than that, though, I think it's because it's really a series about obsession and craft. Most of the chefs have devoted their entire lives to doing one thing as well as it can possibly be done, and there's something quite inspiring about that, whatever field you're in. I often finish an episode feeling slightly more motivated to take my own work seriously.

p3samples9: Has the internet changed the way people watch television?

Fundamentally, yes. The biggest shift is that viewing has become individual and on demand. Instead of a family sitting down at eight o'clock for whatever was scheduled, everyone watches what they want, when they want, often on their own device. That's given people far more choice, and it's made room for niche programmes that would never have survived on traditional channels. But something's been lost too. Fewer shows now become shared national experiences that everyone talks about the next day. And binge-watching has changed storytelling itself, with series designed to be consumed in long sessions rather than week by week.
Will traditional TV channels survive in the future?

In some form, I think they will, but their role is likely to shrink considerably. Younger audiences have largely moved to streaming and online video, and advertising revenue is following them. Where traditional channels still have a real advantage is live content: news, major sporting events and national occasions, where people want to watch at the same moment as everyone else. Public broadcasters may also survive because of their role in providing trusted information. So I'd expect them to become more specialised, focusing on live and local content, rather than disappearing altogether.
